title: How Rainforests Work
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss how tropical rainforests work, drawing on Charles C. Mann's books on human-managed Amazon landscapes. Topics include slash-and-char agriculture and terra preta-style fertile soils, rainforest size and rainfall, the layered structure from forest floor to emergent trees, nutrient-poor soils and buttress roots, epiphytes and strangler plants, biodiversity (tree species, insects, ants), seed dispersal by animals, smuggling of live animals, bat migrations, medicinal plants and food crops that originated in rainforests, deforestation rates and causes (cattle ranching, logging, mining, corporations), and the decline of indigenous peoples. The episode closes with Comic Con and trivia night announcements and a plug for the Amazon Institute's adopt-a-sloth program.

segments.title: Opening banter and Charles C. Mann's Amazon book
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about Charles C. Mann's books arguing the Amazon Basin was human-managed, including slash-and-char agriculture that makes soil more fertile, and note that rainforest soil is generally infertile deep down. They also joke about Emmy and Grammy nominations and introduce Joanne Stand-Alone of the Amazon Institute.

segments.title: Rainforest extent, deforestation rate, and indigenous population decline
segments.summary: Tropical rainforests cover about six to seven percent of dry land but hold a large share of species. At about fifty thousand acres lost per day, a widely cited forty-years-to-zero estimate is described as roughly accurate. The hosts note the Amazonian indigenous population has fallen sharply, and that tropical rainforests span more than eighty countries.

segments.title: Rainfall, temperature, and the equatorial climate
segments.summary: Rainforests receive about 160 to 400 inches of rain a year with no dry season, and temperatures stay hot and muggy. They form a band around the equator, where the sun's angle does not create seasons as it does elsewhere.

segments.title: Rainforest layers: canopy, emergents, and forest floor
segments.summary: The canopy of giant trees, up to about 150 to 200 feet, blocks most light, with only about one percent reaching the forest floor. Emergent trees grow above the canopy. When a canopy gap opens, plants and animals rush toward the light. The forest floor has moss and fungus but little grass.

segments.title: Epiphytes, strangler figs, and lianas
segments.summary: Seedlings must climb a long way to reach light, and many die. Epiphytes such as ferns and orchids grow on large trees for height, and some epiphytes become stranglers that choke their host. Lianas, which depend on other plants to climb, are compared to kudzu.

segments.title: Shallow soils, buttress roots, and nutrient cycling
segments.summary: Heavy rain washes nutrients away, leaving thin fertile soil and shallow roots that make trees prone to falling. Some trees grow buttress roots for support. Bacteria help recycle nutrients for trees.

segments.title: Biodiversity, ants, and seed dispersal
segments.summary: Around three hundred tree species occur in the rainforest, spread widely so each acre holds few of each. Estimates of about ten million animal species are cited, and the hosts say many are being lost daily. Ants are said to make up a large share of rainforest biomass. Insects and birds spread seeds since wind dispersal is limited.

segments.title: Animals, adaptations, and wildlife smuggling
segments.summary: Reptiles and amphibians are abundant, and animals have adaptations such as gliding membranes on flying squirrels and prehensile tails on monkeys. Live animal smuggling is described as the fourth largest smuggling trade. The hosts also describe a Zambian bat migration of about ten million bats to a mango area each October.

segments.title: Medicines, food crops, and the rainforest as pharmacy
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the idea of the rainforest as the world's pharmacy, with about a quarter of medicines derived from rainforest plants and only about one percent of Amazon plants analyzed by Western chemists. Many foods originated in rainforests, including cinnamon, cloves, avocado, pineapple, corn, chocolate, coffee, and tomatoes. Loss of indigenous medicine men's knowledge is discussed.

segments.title: Rainforest oxygen, climate role, and causes of deforestation
segments.summary: The hosts say the rainforest's effect on world oxygen is not a net contribution, though it absorbs heat and affects temperature. Deforestation is driven by clearing for lumber, paper, and cattle pasture. Cleared soil lasts only a year or two for crops. Cattle ranching is said to yield much more per acre than timber, and corporations and violence against indigenous people are discussed.

segments.title: Live show and trivia night announcements
segments.summary: Hosts announce a live show at Comic Con in New York on October 12 and a trivia night at the Cutting Room in the Flatiron District, with doors at 7:30 and trivia at 8:30.

segments.title: Amazon Institute adopt-a-sloth plug
segments.summary: The hosts promote the Amazon Institute, which describes nutritional education and food exchanges that replace hunting monkeys and sloths. A seventy-five dollar donation adopts a sloth and includes a certificate and a CD of rainforest sounds, with classroom programs also offered.

segments.title: Sign-off and contact information
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners and give contact details for Twitter, Facebook, and email, and point to HowStuffWorks for more on rainforests.
